items.question: "The composition of the UN Security Council reflects the geopolitics of 1945, not of today." In this context, examine the case for India's permanent membership and the obstacles to Security Council reform.
items.modelAnswer:
The **UN Security Council (UNSC)**, with its **five permanent veto-wielding members (USA, UK, France, Russia, China)** and ten elected non-permanent members, was designed around the victors of the Second World War. Eight decades on, critics argue it under-represents Asia, Africa and Latin America and lacks legitimacy for a membership of 193 states.

**The case for India.** India is the world's most populous nation and a major economy, the largest troop contributor to UN peacekeeping over time, a responsible nuclear power, and a consistent voice for the Global South. It anchors the **G4 (with Japan, Germany and Brazil)**, which seeks expansion of both permanent and non-permanent categories; the African bloc's parallel demand is the **Ezulwini Consensus**. India has served several terms as a non-permanent member and enjoys broad support from the P5 barring reservations from China.

**Obstacles.** Reform requires a **Charter amendment** — a two-thirds UNGA vote plus ratification by two-thirds of members **including all P5**, giving each permanent member an effective veto over change. Rival blocs stall progress: the **"Uniting for Consensus" group** (Italy, Pakistan and others) opposes new permanent seats; there is no agreement on **whether new members would have the veto**; and negotiations remain stuck in a text-less **Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN)** process.

**Conclusion.** Meaningful reform demands sustained coalition-building, a willingness to accept incremental change (e.g., a longer-term renewable seat), and pressure to make the IGN text-based and time-bound. For India, the strategic path lies in leveraging its **G20 leadership and Global South diplomacy** to convert widespread rhetorical support into concrete negotiating outcomes.
keyPoints: UNSC = P5 (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) with veto + 10 non-permanent members; frozen 1945 design.
India's case: population, economy, peacekeeping record, responsible nuclear power, Global South voice; anchors the G4.
African demand = Ezulwini Consensus; G4 = India, Japan, Germany, Brazil.
Reform needs a Charter amendment ratified by all P5 — an effective veto on change.
'Uniting for Consensus' bloc opposes new permanent seats; veto-extension and text-based IGN are unresolved.
Way forward: coalition-building, incremental options, and leveraging India's G20/Global South leadership.
items.source: UN Charter (un.org); MEA (mea.gov.in) on UNSC reform — verified Sep 2026

items.question: Discuss the roles of the IMF, the World Bank and the WTO in global economic governance, and evaluate why emerging economies have created alternative institutions such as the AIIB and the New Development Bank.
items.modelAnswer:
Global economic governance rests on three post-war pillars. The **IMF** (Bretton Woods, 1944; HQ Washington) safeguards monetary stability and offers **balance-of-payments support**; the **World Bank Group** (IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA, ICSID) finances **development and poverty reduction**; and the **WTO** (successor to the GATT since 1995; HQ Geneva) frames trade rules and runs a **binding dispute-settlement mechanism**. Together they shape lending conditionality, development finance and the trading order.

**Grievances of emerging economies.** Voting power in the IMF and World Bank remains skewed towards advanced economies, and leadership follows an outdated convention (a **European IMF Managing Director** and an **American World Bank President**). Quota reforms have lagged behind the rising weight of countries like India and China; WTO negotiations (the Doha Round) stalled, and its Appellate Body was paralysed by member disputes.

**Alternative institutions.** The **AIIB** (2016, HQ Beijing) and the **BRICS New Development Bank** (HQ Shanghai, led by Dilma Rousseff) were created to widen infrastructure finance with more balanced voting for developing members. They are best seen as **complements rather than rivals** — the AIIB co-finances projects with the World Bank and ADB — while signalling a demand for a more multipolar order.

**AP / India angle.** India is a founding member of the **AIIB and NDB** and a leading borrower from the ADB and World Bank; multilateral loans support infrastructure and urban projects across Indian states, including Andhra Pradesh. India uses these platforms alongside its **G20 presidency** to press for quota reform and a stronger Global South voice.

**Conclusion.** The new banks have expanded the pool of development finance without displacing the Bretton Woods system; the durable solution is reform of quotas, leadership selection and the WTO dispute mechanism to reflect twenty-first-century economic realities.
keyPoints: IMF = monetary stability/BoP support; World Bank = development finance (IBRD/IDA/IFC/MIGA/ICSID); WTO = trade rules + dispute settlement.
Emerging-economy grievances: skewed IMF/WB voting, dated leadership convention, stalled Doha Round, paralysed WTO Appellate Body.
AIIB (2016, Beijing) and NDB (BRICS, Shanghai) offer infrastructure finance with more balanced voting.
New banks are complements, not rivals — AIIB co-finances with the World Bank and ADB.
India is a founding member of AIIB and NDB and a major ADB/World Bank borrower supporting state-level projects.
Durable fix = quota reform, leadership-selection reform, and restoring WTO dispute settlement.
items.source: IMF (imf.org); World Bank (worldbank.org); WTO (wto.org); AIIB (aiib.org); NDB (ndb.int) — verified Sep 2026
